question.title: Anti-inflammatory Food
question.text: Nutrition researchers increasingly focus on overall eating patterns rather than treating one food as a simple cure for inflammation. Diets rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts and unsaturated oils tend to provide fibre and nutrients while limiting heavily processed foods.
keyPoints: Nutrition researchers increasingly focus on overall eating patterns rather than treating one food as a simple cure for inflammation.
Diets rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts and unsaturated oils tend to provide fibre and nutrients while limiting heavily processed foods.
Seasonal produce can be useful because it is often fresh and varied, although seasonality itself does not automatically make a food anti-inflammatory.
What matters most is the repeated combination of foods across meals and the extent to which the diet replaces excess refined sugar, salt and saturated fat.

question.title: Soot and black carbon
question.text: Sometimes it's the little things that can make big things happen. Fleas and the plague, atoms and nuclear bombs. Diminutive leaders in world history. Soot is one of these little things. Soot, also known as black carbon, is released when you burn dung, coal, diesel fuel and wood. From Los Angeles to Mumbai, soot causes respiratory illnesses like lung cancer and asthma and contributes to one point six million premature deaths every year, mostly among the poor. And it gets worse. Atmospheric currents carry soot thousands of miles from where it is produced, to the Himalayas and the Arctic. Black carbon, being black, absorbs sunlight, so even a little soot on snow makes it melt faster. And when snow melts, global sea levels rise, threatening our freshwater, indigenous communities and polar bears who hunt on the Arctic ice. Climate change has been a big thing for a while and carbon dioxide has been its main cause. Scientists estimate that soot causes twenty-five percent of human-caused global warming. It's the second leading cause of Arctic warming after carbon dioxide. Let's not underestimate the impact of this tiny particle. But there's good news: reducing black carbon may be the fastest way to slow global warming. Buy time for the Arctic. Yes, even more so than changing a light bulb. Since black carbon only stays in the atmosphere for a couple of weeks, reducing it will produce results immediately.
facts: Black carbon or soot is released by burning dung, coal, diesel and wood.
The speaker links soot with respiratory disease and premature deaths, particularly among poorer people.
Air currents carry soot to snow-covered regions where it absorbs sunlight and accelerates melting.
The lecture describes a major contribution to warming and argues that cutting this short-lived pollutant can bring rapid benefits.
question.sample: The lecture explains how soot, or black carbon, has large effects despite its tiny size. Burning fuels releases soot, which contributes to respiratory illnesses and premature deaths. Atmospheric currents transport it to the Himalayas and the Arctic, where it absorbs sunlight and makes snow melt faster. The speaker also describes its contribution to global warming. Because black carbon stays in the atmosphere for only a few weeks, reducing emissions could deliver rapid benefits.

question.title: Morton Prince and multiple personalities
question.text: Morton Prince was an American physician and psychologist; his book, Dissociation of a Personality, was the best-seller at that time. It tells the story of Miss Christine Beauchamp, who was suffering from MPD, Multiple Personality Disorder. Miss Beauchamp had several personalities, namely B1, B2 and B3. There was a hidden memory in these three personalities. Miss Beauchamp was B2. B2 knows about B1, B3 knows both B1 and B2, but B1 knows nothing about B2 or B3. The strongest personality accounts for most of the time, and it will take over the others and become the main personality at the end. This case and theory give great help to crime investigation. The Beetle, featuring menacing foreign mesmerists, hypnotising villains, somnambulistic criminals and spectacular dissociations of personality. Such figures and tropes were not merely the stuff of Gothic fiction, however; from 1875 to the close of the century, cases of dual or multiple personality were reported with increasing frequency.

The passage describes B1, B2 and B3 with different access to memories of the other personalities.
The speaker describes a dominant personality and a connection with crime investigation.
The passage connects dissociation with Gothic fiction such as The Beetle and increasingly frequent late-nineteenth-century reports.

question.instruction: Listen to the three speakers once. Prepare for 10 seconds, then summarise their discussion within two minutes.
question.title: Campus part-time jobs
question.narration: Three students are debating the pros and cons of campus part-time jobs, gathered at a corner table in the student lounge, the air filled with the faint smell of coffee and the rustle of textbook pages.
turns: Speaker 1

I think working part-time on campus is a total waste of energy. Last month I took a job at the library desk, and between shelving books and scanning IDs, I barely had any mental capacity left for my coursework. I ended up dozing off during my morning lectures twice last week.
Speaker 2

Actually, I find my part-time job at the academic office really helpful. It forces me to manage my time better. I used to procrastinate all afternoon, but now I block out my shifts and study hours in advance. Plus, I'm earning my own spending money it feels good not to have to ask my parents for every little thing.
Speaker 3

But the workload is no joke. I tried working at the campus café last semester and it drained me completely. Some days I'd finish my shift at 8 pm, and then still have to write a lab report due at midnight. I got so stressed I had to quit after a month. It's not just about time it's the mental toll.
Speaker 1

Exactly! And let's be honest most of these jobs don't even relate to our future careers. I'd rather join a student club or work on a project that actually builds my resume. Stuffing envelopes or swiping cards isn't going to help me get into grad school.
Speaker 2

I see what you mean, but you're overlooking the soft skills. I've learned to talk to supervisors, handle complaints, and show up on time that's real-world experience. And it's not always about the job itself; it's about showing you can balance responsibilities.
Speaker 3

I guess, but I still think it depends on your schedule. If you're taking 18 credits like I am this semester, adding a job is just unrealistic. The stress isn't sustainable. Maybe if the university limited work hours to under 10 per week... but even then, I'd rather use that time to review or sleep.
Speaker 1

Same. I'd prefer a work-study program that's more flexible and aligned with my major. Maybe assisting a professor with research instead of stacking books. That way I'm earning and learning at the same time. Otherwise, it just feels like trading precious study hours for tasks that don't contribute to my long-term goals.
Speaker 2

That's a fair point. I wouldn't say no to a more relevant job either. But still, even a simple job teaches discipline. And let's be real not all of us can get those research assistant roles. Sometimes starting with a basic job can actually open doors to those better opportunities later on.
Speaker 3

Well, if I'm going to work, I'd want it to mean something beyond the pay check. Otherwise, I'd rather focus on my grades. There has to be a balance. Burnout is real, and no amount of money is worth compromising both my health and academic performance.
facts: The discussion weighs campus part-time jobs against study demands and wellbeing.
Speaker 1 finds library work exhausting and insufficiently related to future career goals.
Speaker 1 would prefer flexible work-study or research assistance aligned with their major.
Speaker 2 says office work improves time management, financial independence, communication, reliability and discipline.
Speaker 2 accepts that relevant work is preferable but argues basic jobs can lead to better opportunities.
Speaker 3 describes café work causing stress, quitting after a month, and an unsustainable workload with 18 credits.
Speaker 3 prioritises health and grades and considers limited hours, while the group recognises the need for balance without fully agreeing on the value of campus work.
question.sample: The students discuss whether campus part-time jobs are worthwhile. The first speaker says library work drains energy and offers little career relevance, preferring flexible work connected to their major, such as research assistance. The second values office work for income, better time management and transferable skills, arguing that basic jobs can also lead to better opportunities. The third describes quitting a café job because of stress and conflicting deadlines, and believes heavy study loads leave little room for employment. Although more relevant work appeals to the group, their views remain different. The discussion highlights balancing income and experience against academic performance and health.

question.title: Complaints
question.text:
Humans love to complain to each other. It helps us feel less alone. Think about what happens when a family member or friend is going through a tough time; they call up someone who will listen to their tale of woe. Unfortunately, negative bonding is the default for many groups.

In some families, complaining is the only way to get attention. When one person says, I had a bad day; the other person has to top it, "You think you had a tough day. I had to do three TPS reports!" The same thing happens at work and social settings. "Your child didn't sleep through the night until 6 months? Mine was a full year old before she went over six hours." It's a race to the bottom, and the worst situation wins.

In Bitching is Bonding, A Guide To Mutual Complaint, Irene S. Levine, Ph.D., a professor of psychiatry at the NYU Langone School of Medicine says, "The reason why these conversations feel good is because we feel understood."

People raised in negative environments learn early on. Being positive gets you thrown out of the club. When family dinner is a complaint fest, you're not going to risk alienation saying, "Wow, I had an awesome day. Don't you just love life?"

Translate this into a work setting: people, often unconsciously, believe being positive keeps you out of the cool club. When negativity provides bonding, humans are reluctant to abandon the behavior that brings them comfort.
keyPoints: Complaining can function as a form of social bonding by making people feel understood.
Families and work groups may reward negative stories and competitive expressions of hardship.
Group norms can discourage positive comments because members fear exclusion.
People resist abandoning negativity when it provides social comfort and belonging.
question.sample: Complaining can help people feel understood and connected, but repeated negative bonding in families and workplaces can turn hardship into competition and discourage positivity through fear of exclusion, so individuals may continue expressing negativity even when it is unhelpful because belonging to the group feels comforting.

question.title: Education Technology
question.text:
In 1953 B.F. Skinner visited his daughter's maths class. The Harvard psychologist found every pupil learning the same topic in the same way at the same speed. A few days later he built his first "teaching machine", which let children tackle questions at their own pace. By the mid-1960s similar gizmos were being flogged by door-to-door salesmen. Within a few years, though, enthusiasm for them had fizzled out.

Since then education technology (edtech) has repeated the cycle of hype and flop, even as computers have reshaped almost every other part of life. One reason is the conservatism of teachers and their unions. But another is that the brain-stretching potential of edtech has remained unproven.

Today, however, Skinner's heirs are forcing the sceptics to think again (see article). Backed by billionaire techies such as Mark Zuckerberg and Bill Gates, schools around the world are using new software to "personalize" learning. This could help hundreds of millions of children stuck in dismal classes—but only if edtech boosters can resist the temptation to revive harmful ideas about how children learn. To succeed, edtech must be at the service of teaching, not the other way around.

The conventional model of schooling emerged in Prussia in the 18th century. Alternatives have so far failed to teach as many children as efficiently. Classrooms, hierarchical year-groups, standardized curriculums and fixed timetables are still the norm for most of the world's nearly 1.5bn schoolchildren.
keyPoints: Educational technology has long promised personalised learning, beginning with Skinner’s teaching machine.
Repeated enthusiasm has faded because effectiveness remains uncertain and traditional teaching structures persist.
Modern software may adapt learning pace but must be guided by sound teaching principles.
Edtech could improve education at scale if it serves pedagogy rather than dictating it.
question.sample: Educational technology has repeatedly promised to personalise learning since Skinner’s teaching machine, but its benefits remain disputed and conventional schooling persists; although modern software could support millions of students, success depends on evidence-based approaches that place technology in service of effective teaching rather than allowing tools to dictate educational methods.

question.title: Combining Study and Employment
question.text: Effective study requires time, comfort and peace. It is impossible to study with employment because one may distract the other. To what extent do you think the statements are realistic? Give your opinion with examples.
keyPoints: Give a clear opinion about whether employment and effective study can coexist.
Discuss how employment can create time pressure, tiredness or distraction.
Explain possible benefits such as discipline, income and practical skills.
Support the view with realistic examples and conditions for success.
question.sample:
The claim that employment makes effective study impossible is too absolute. Working while studying can create serious pressure, but many students can manage both when their hours are limited and their schedules are organised carefully.

Employment may reduce the time and energy available for academic work. A student who finishes a late shift may struggle to concentrate during an early lecture or may postpone important assignments. Unpredictable rosters can be especially damaging because the learner cannot plan regular revision. Financial concerns may also distract students from their studies. These problems show why full-time employment is often unsuitable during demanding courses.

Nevertheless, part-time work can provide useful advantages. Earning an income may reduce dependence on family members and allow a student to pay for transport, books or accommodation. A job can also develop punctuality, communication and problem-solving skills. For instance, a student working several fixed hours in a shop may learn to plan study periods efficiently and become more disciplined about deadlines.

In my experience, combining study with a small weekend job was manageable because my shifts were predictable. I reserved weekday evenings for reading and began assignments before they became urgent. The arrangement became difficult only when I accepted extra shifts during examination periods. This taught me that the number and timing of hours matter more than employment itself. Therefore, study and employment can coexist, provided students have realistic workloads, protected study time and an employer willing to respect their academic commitments.

question.text: People differ in how strongly their moods change, with some experiencing sharp emotional swings and others remaining comparatively steady. question.title: Citizens collecting scientific data
question.text: Scientific research sometimes requires observations from more places than a small professional team can visit. Volunteers can help by recording birds, measuring rainfall or photographing changes along a coastline. Their contribution can reveal patterns across wide areas and long periods. However, collecting more observations does not automatically produce reliable evidence. Participants need clear instructions about what to record and how to report uncertainty. For example, a volunteer who cannot identify a bird should be able to mark the observation as uncertain instead of guessing. Researchers also need to consider where observations come from. Easily accessible parks may receive many visits, while remote locations remain poorly represented. Training, checks by experienced observers and careful analysis can reduce these problems, although they cannot remove every source of error. There is also an educational benefit: participants learn how scientific questions are investigated and why conclusions sometimes change. This benefit is stronger when researchers share results and explain how the observations were used. Citizen science therefore works best as a partnership, combining public participation with professional guidance, transparent methods and continuing communication.
question.prompt: Which TWO measures help make volunteer observations reliable?
choices: Asking volunteers to guess uncertain identifications.
Allowing participants to report uncertainty.
Providing clear recording instructions.
Assuming that a larger dataset removes all error.
Collecting only in easily accessible parks.

question.title: A shared tool workshop
question.text: A neighbourhood workshop lends tools and provides space for small repair projects. When it first opened, members were encouraged to leave comments in a suggestion box. The organisers received many requests for new equipment and almost ordered several expensive machines. Before doing so, they examined the booking records and spoke to members who rarely visited. This revealed a different problem. Several tools were already available, but their names in the catalogue were unfamiliar and their storage locations were unclear. New members often assumed that the workshop did not own what they needed. The organisers improved the catalogue with photographs and short descriptions. They also introduced a regular orientation session in which members practised finding and returning equipment. Demand for some proposed purchases then fell because existing tools became easier to locate. This did not mean that new equipment was unnecessary. It meant that purchasing decisions could be based on a clearer picture of what members actually lacked. The workshop continued to record requests, but it considered them alongside observed use, maintenance costs and the training required for safe operation. The main lesson was that improving access to existing resources can sometimes solve a problem more effectively than increasing the amount of equipment.

Ordering every machine mentioned in the suggestion box.
Considering requests alongside use and maintenance needs.
Examining booking records and speaking to infrequent users.
question.explanation: Records and conversations revealed access problems; requests were then evaluated with use, maintenance and safety training.

question.title: Making buses dependable
question.text: When a city wants more people to use buses, reducing the ticket price may seem the obvious first step. Fares matter, but passengers also consider whether a service is dependable. If a bus arrives unpredictably, someone travelling to work may need to leave much earlier than the journey itself requires. Frequent, reliable services reduce this uncertainty. Dedicated lanes can help buses avoid traffic, while well-designed stops can make boarding quicker and easier. Connections deserve attention too. A short journey on one route may still be inconvenient if a passenger faces a long wait for the next bus. Timetables and information should therefore describe the whole journey rather than isolated routes. Improvements also need to reach neighbourhoods where people depend on public transport most. Counting total passenger numbers alone could overlook these areas if they have smaller populations. Planners should listen to existing users and people who currently find the network difficult to use. A successful bus system combines reasonable fares, consistent journey times and accessible connections. The goal is to make public transport a practical everyday choice, not merely to advertise an inexpensive ticket.

question.explanation: Affordable fares are not enough: dedicated lanes, efficient stops, connections and inclusive planning make journeys dependable.

question.title: Preserving digital records
question.text: A box of old letters can remain readable for many years if the paper survives. A digital collection presents a different challenge. Even when a file is undamaged, the software or equipment needed to open it may no longer be available. Digital preservation therefore means more than keeping a backup copy. Organisations need to know what their files contain, which formats they use and who is permitted to access them. Descriptive information makes records easier to find and interpret, especially when the people who created them have left. Copies stored in different locations protect against a single equipment failure, but these copies should also be checked regularly. Moving information into a newer format can preserve access, although staff must verify that important features have not been lost in the process. There are choices about priorities because storing everything indefinitely can be expensive and difficult to manage. Records should be selected according to their lasting value and the organisation's responsibilities. The central lesson is that digital preservation is an ongoing activity requiring planning, documentation and review, rather than a task completed by purchasing additional storage.

question.explanation: The emphasis is continuing usability, rather than storage alone, through maintenance, migration and prioritisation.

question.text: Volunteers creating a local history map began by recording the place names used by older residents.
